papers.summary: Perplexity releases 0.6B and 9B multi-vector retrievers that encode text, images, and document screenshots: each document token stores a 128-d vector, and scoring sums MaxSim of each query vector against document vectors. deep_reading.title: pplx-embed-v2-late Technical Report
deep_reading.content:
Perplexity has released two multi-vector retrieval models, pplx-embed-v2-late, at 0.6B and 9B parameters, which encode text, images and screenshots of document pages. They are "late-interaction" retrievers: every document token is stored as a 128-dimensional vector, every query token also gets its own vector, and scoring takes, for each query vector, the largest inner product with any document vector, then sums those maxima (MaxSim). The two models are not trained separately with contrastive learning. Instead ==both imitate, token by token, the vectors produced by the same 18B teacher==, so they land in the same embedding space: a document collection can be indexed offline with the 9B model and queried online with the 0.6B model, scoring directly. On 72 domain retrieval tasks assembled by the authors, the 9B model averages 81.3% nDCG@10, 1.6 points above the runner-up nemotron-3-embed-8b. A 0.6B query against a 9B document index scores 79.6%, 1.6 points above using 0.6B on both sides, at the same query-side cost. This is a short technical report, and the credibility of its main results has to be judged piece by piece. The task list of the domain benchmark is not public, and the labels of the two production benchmarks partly come from Perplexity's own production system; only ViDoRe-V3 and BrowseComp+ can be reproduced independently.

## 1. Why late interaction, and why distillation

Retrieval models usually trade off between two designs. Single-vector models compress a whole document into one vector, which is fast with approximate nearest-neighbor search but loses detail. Cross-encoders run the query and document through the model together, which works well but needs a separate pass per candidate, so they are only usable for reranking. Late interaction sits in between: document token vectors are computed offline and stored, at query time only the query's vectors are computed, and MaxSim does the scoring. The price is storage, which is why this work compresses each token vector to 128 dimensions.

The authors' other judgment is that small models trained directly with contrastive learning fall short, and fitting the token vectors of a large model works better, especially at small sizes. A by-product is that students of different sizes distilled from the same teacher are interchangeable. The report body, however, gives no numbers comparing distillation with direct contrastive training, so for now this is the authors' experience only.

## 2. Training pipeline

### 2.1 The 18B teacher: two-stage contrastive learning

The teacher is Qwen3.5-27B with its last 20 layers pruned, giving 18B, and with the causal mask removed from the attention layers so every token sees both sides of its context. Training has two stages.

The first stage uses query–document pairs. The data come from 28 datasets, further split by language and domain into 981 subsets, 186M pairs in total. 88.3% are text–text, 8.3% text–image and 3.4% text–document-screenshot, and 14M of the text pairs are synthesized by generating queries backward from PDF passages. Sampling weights are adjusted during training to change the three proportions to 56.5%, 30.9% and 12.6%, heavily upsampling images and screenshots. Each batch is drawn from a single subset, so the other documents in the batch (the negatives) are closer to the positive and harder to tell apart. To make subsets appear in their target proportions and at evenly spaced intervals, the authors do not draw independently at each step. They cut 0 to 1 into 981 segments, each as long as its subset's sampling share, with subsets from the same source placed next to each other. At step $n$ they take the fractional part of "random start $+\,n\times0.618\ldots$" (0.618 being the inverse golden ratio), and the segment it lands in supplies that batch. These points cover 0 to 1 very evenly, so each segment is hit about as often as its length and the hits are spread out in time; subsets from one source form one long segment, so "proportional and evenly spaced" also holds at the source level. The contrastive batch is 16,384 pairs, trained with LoRA (rank 128). In-batch documents whose MaxSim score is within 0.2 of the positive's are not counted as negatives, to reduce false negatives. MaxSim is written as a Triton kernel to avoid materializing the token-level similarity matrix.

The second stage merges the LoRA weights, adds a new rank-32 adapter, freezes the vision part and trains on text triplets only: each query gets one positive and up to 4 hard negatives. Some hard negatives are synthesized by changing key information in highly templated documents, for instance a financial report in a fixed format with a single number changed, which forces the model to read details.

### 2.2 Students: fitting the teacher's vectors token by token

The student loss is direct. For every valid query and document token, take the Euclidean distance between the student vector and the teacher vector (both L2-normalized), average the query part and the document part separately, and add them. The teacher is not updated.

$$\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{Q}}\lVert q^S_{it}-q^T_{it}\rVert_2+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(i,t)\in\mathcal{D}}\lVert d^S_{it}-d^T_{it}\rVert_2$$

Because this loss does not rely on in-batch negatives, a batch can mix several subsets, which steadies the gradient. The 9B student is based on Qwen3.5-9B. The authors found LoRA alone could not fit well enough, and they guess that token-level alignment constrains the whole embedding space too tightly. So they fully fine-tune the last 8 layers of the text part and use LoRA elsewhere. The 0.6B student is pruned from Qwen3.5-0.8B, removing 2 of the 3 linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet) layers in each block. It ends up with 594M parameters in total, of which 254M are the token-embedding table and 100M the image encoder, so about 240M are actually active for text. It is fully fine-tuned, because full fine-tuning clearly beat training adapters only on document-screenshot tasks.

## 3. Experiments

### 3.1 Text retrieval

The domain benchmark consists of 72 public tasks covering finance, legal, health, conversation, tech and multilingual, with task counts ranging from 4 in tech to 20 in legal. The metric is nDCG@10, averaged with equal weight over the six domains:

| Model | Dim | Avg | Finance | Legal | Health | Conv. | Tech | Multiling. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pplx-embed-v2-late-9b | 128 multi | **81.3** | 82.5 | 81.6 | 82.5 | 81.5 | 70.4 | 89.5 |
| nemotron-3-embed-8b | 4096 single | 79.7 | 80.8 | 81.1 | 83.9 | 77.4 | 67.5 | 87.9 |
| voyage-4-large | 1024 single | 79.0 | 81.5 | 80.0 | 83.0 | 76.7 | 65.1 | 87.9 |
| pplx-embed-v2-late-0.6b | 128 multi | 78.0 | 79.9 | 78.2 | 78.0 | 79.7 | 66.6 | 85.8 |
| voyage-4-nano | 2048 single | 74.6 | 77.3 | 75.8 | 76.0 | 74.7 | 59.4 | 84.3 |
| qwen3-embedding-0.6b | 1024 single | 68.4 | 67.9 | 70.0 | 72.4 | 68.4 | 53.9 | 77.8 |

The 9B model is best in every domain except health; the 0.6B model is best among sub-1B models in every domain. The 9B model's largest leads are in conversation (+4.1) and tech (+2.9), domains with only 5 and 4 tasks, where a single task's swing moves the average a lot. In legal, the domain with the most tasks, 9B is only 0.5 above nemotron. The authors withhold the task list so that later models cannot tune to it. The reason is understandable, but the cost is that this table cannot be checked.

Q2D-Web is closer to Perplexity's production setting: about 70,000 agent-rewritten production search queries over a corpus of 190M web pages, measured by Recall@1000. Relevant documents have three kinds of labels: documents the agent cited in its answer; documents the production retrieval system ranked high; and the union of those two, extended with documents an LLM judged relevant. The table compares the two pplx models with the strongest baselines:

| Model | Cited by agent | Ranked high by production system | Combined (plus LLM judgments) |
|---|---|---|---|
| pplx-embed-v2-late-9b | 88.2 | 68.8 | 74.8 |
| pplx-embed-v2-late-0.6b | 86.7 | 67.3 | 73.6 |
| nemotron-3-embed-8b | 83.1 | 61.7 | 69.3 |
| qwen3-embedding-8b | 79.3 | 58.3 | 65.3 |

The second column treats documents ranked high by Perplexity's production retrieval as relevant, which naturally favors models that rank like the production system, and the pplx models lead nemotron most in this column (7.1 points). The authors therefore emphasize the combined labels, which they say reduce this bias. But the first column, "documents cited by the agent", also comes out of the production system's search results and carries the same lean, so none of the three columns is fully neutral. Even so, the 0.6B model beats the 8B nemotron in all three columns, which shows the advantage is not all label bias.

The report also tests the text version of ViDoRe-V3, where document page screenshots are converted to Markdown by OCR before retrieval, again scored by nDCG@10. The 9B model scores 64.7%, the 0.6B 61.2%, and the best baseline, nemotron, 60.6%. This is the only text result that can be reproduced independently.

### 3.2 Document-screenshot and image retrieval

All three benchmarks below are text-to-image retrieval, scored by nDCG@10 (%).

| Model | Dim per token | ViDoRe-V3 (screenshots) | MIRACL-Vision | PPLX-Q2I |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pplx-embed-v2-late-9b | 128 | 65.2 | 75.7 | 65.0 |
| pplx-embed-v2-late-0.6b | 128 | 62.3 | 67.5 | 60.4 |
| topk-embed-v1-2b | 128 | 61.9 | 60.2 | 51.5 |
| gemini-embedding-2 | 3072 (single vector) | 46.0 | **77.5** | **67.0** |
| qwen3-vl-embedding-8b | 4096 (single vector) | 58.3 | 68.5 | 50.6 |
| evie-8b (image retrieval only) | 4096 | **66.4** | – | – |

On images it does not lead across the board. On ViDoRe-V3, EVIE (a vision-only multi-vector model) trained specifically for image retrieval scores higher in both its 8B and 4.5B versions, at 66.4% and 65.9%. But they store 4,096 and 2,048 dimensions per token, ==while pplx-embed-v2-late stores only 128==, so the gap has to be read together with storage cost.

The fairest comparison is topk-embed-v1, also at 128 dimensions: the 0.6B model is 0.4 points above the 2B topk model, while topk at its full 2,048 dimensions is 0.9 points above the 0.6B model. That means under the same storage budget, pplx's small model matches a model of the same kind with more than three times the parameters. On MIRACL-Vision (Wikipedia page screenshots) and PPLX-Q2I (Perplexity's production image-search logs, 10,000 queries and 100,000 images), gemini-embedding-2 scores higher. PPLX-Q2I defines relevant images as "images actually served in production", carrying the same production-system lean as Q2D-Web. EVIE and Nemotron ColEmbed were not evaluated on this set; the authors say their dimensions are too high to make indexing practical.

### 3.3 Small-model queries + large-model index

![nDCG@10 of three query/document model pairings across six domains (paper Figure 2). Dark blue: 9B on both sides; medium blue: 0.6B queries against 9B documents; light blue: 0.6B on both sides.](figs/2610.29523/fig2_cross_model.png)

Documents are indexed with the 9B model, and queries are encoded with either 9B or 0.6B. A 0.6B query against 9B documents beats 0.6B on both sides in all six domains, raising the average from 78.0% to 79.6%; 9B on both sides scores 81.3%. In other words, switching only the document side recovers almost half of the 9B model's 3.3-point advantage over 0.6B. Query encoding costs the same as pure 0.6B, and the cost of indexing documents is amortized over the life of the index. The report runs this experiment only on the domain benchmark, not on Q2D-Web or the image tasks.

### 3.4 As the retriever for a search agent

![Answer accuracy (left) and retrieval recall (right) on BrowseComp+, against the average number of searches; top-left is better (paper Figure 3).](figs/2610.29523/fig3_browsecomp.png)

BrowseComp+ has GPT-OSS-120B act as an agent that repeatedly searches a fixed corpus with the retriever under test to answer complex questions, and another LLM grades the answers. The 9B model reaches 64.0% accuracy, 4.9 points above the other late-interaction model, Reason-ModernColBERT, and 8.7 points above the best single-vector model, voyage-4-large. ==It also needs fewer searches on average than every baseline==, and its recall is highest too. A more accurate retriever lets the agent search fewer rounds, a direct cost saving for search agents billed per call.

## 4. Limitations

The report gives no storage or latency figures, and these are the main cost of late interaction. A rough calculation at the training truncation length: a 1,000-token document stores 128,000 numbers, about 256 KB in half precision. A 1,024-dimensional single vector in half precision takes only 2 KB, about 128 times less. Real systems usually quantize or cluster token vectors; the report does not say what Perplexity does, nor what MaxSim retrieval latency is over 190M web pages. Also, the domain benchmark's task list is not public and cannot be reproduced; the labels of the two production benchmarks lean toward the production system; "distillation beats direct contrastive learning" lacks comparison numbers; and on image retrieval, dedicated vision models and gemini-embedding-2 are still better on some benchmarks.

## 5. Practical implications

For retrieval teams, the most directly usable idea is "index with the large model, query with the small one": document-side compute is spent once, query-side latency is that of a 0.6B model, and quality is 1.6 points above the small model alone. This requires both models to be distilled from the same teacher; two independently trained models cannot be mixed like this. The 0.6B version has only about 240M active parameters for text, and the authors think it can run on edge devices. If you are evaluating multi-vector retrieval, first measure storage overhead and retrieval latency on your own corpus, and rely mainly on public benchmarks such as ViDoRe-V3. Those are the parts the report either does not answer or that cannot be verified.

papers.title: Directional Posterior Feedback Fusion for Query Reformulation in Dense Retrieval
papers.authors: Yiteng Tu, Qingyi Pan, Weihang Su, Jiaxin Mao, Yiqun Liu, Qingyao Ai
papers.summary: When rewriting a query vector with first-round retrieved documents or an LLM-written hypothetical answer (HyDE), the usual approach averages feedback vectors and interpolates with the original query. DIFF argues that ==each piece of feedback only supports correcting the query along one direction, so other directions should not be pulled back by it==: it subtracts the component parallel to the original query to get each feedback's rotation direction and magnitude, constrains only the projection of the correction onto that direction, weights by query–feedback similarity and group agreement, and solves a K×K linear system—without training any model. On 14 BEIR subsets, bge-base with HyDE rises from 0.5492 to 0.5717 mean NDCG@10; with retrieved-document feedback, vector averaging falls to 0.5045 while DIFF scores 0.5522.

deep_reading.title: Directional Posterior Feedback Fusion for Query Reformulation in Dense Retrieval
deep_reading.content:
In dense retrieval, short queries often under-specify what the user wants. A common fix is to obtain some "feedback" text first, such as the top documents from a first retrieval pass or a hypothetical answer written by an LLM (HyDE), and use it to modify the query vector. Most existing methods average the feedback vectors or interpolate them with the original query. That treats every feedback item as "what the new query should look like" and pulls the query toward it as a whole. This Tsinghua paper proposes DIFF (Directional Posterior Feedback Fusion) and argues that this causes interference: ==a feedback item usually supports a correction along one direction only, yet it also pulls the query back along every direction it says nothing about==. DIFF first computes the direction each feedback item adds relative to the original query and requires the corrected query to agree with the feedback only along that direction, leaving other directions free. It then weights each constraint by feedback quality and adds a "don't move too far from the original query" term as a safeguard. The whole procedure has a closed-form solution and trains no model. On 14 BEIR subsets, 3 retrievers and 4 feedback sources, DIFF has the highest average NDCG@10 in all 12 settings. But with first-pass retrieved documents as feedback it barely improves on the original query without feedback. With LLM-generated feedback, its lead over the strongest baseline, AnchorQE, is about as large as the swing from hyperparameter choice. So the paper's more reliable contribution is "not being dragged down by noisy feedback", not "significantly better retrieval".

![Two fusion styles (paper Figure 1). Left: pointwise fitting, the correction δ is pulled to the middle of two feedback items e₁, e₂. Right: directional constraints, each feedback item only constrains δ's projection on its own direction, so δ can satisfy both.](figs/2610.29464/fig1_point_vs_direction.png)

## 1. The problem: treating feedback as target points loses complementary information

Let the original query vector be $q$, and let feedback item $i$ propose a correction $e_i=\ell_i u_i$ relative to $q$, where $u_i$ is a direction (unit vector) and $\ell_i$ a magnitude. Pointwise fitting wants the correction $\delta$ to be close to $e_i$, i.e. it minimizes $\lVert\delta-\ell_i u_i\rVert^2$. The authors split this into two terms:

$$\lVert\delta-\ell_i u_i\rVert^2=(u_i^\top\delta-\ell_i)^2+\lVert(I-u_iu_i^\top)\delta\rVert^2$$

The first term asks $\delta$'s component along $u_i$ to equal $\ell_i$, which is what we want. The second penalizes $\delta$'s components along all other directions, which may be exactly the corrections other feedback items support. For example, take the query "Apple launch event": one feedback document is about a new phone, another about a new computer. Pointwise fitting pulls the query to the middle, going only halfway in each direction.

The authors prove in the appendix that with equal weights, the correction from directional constraints is never smaller than from pointwise fitting, with equality only when all feedback directions are collinear. The difference is largest when the feedback directions are mutually orthogonal. Under directional constraints the correction along direction $j$ is $\tau_j\ell_j/(\lambda+\tau_j)$; under pointwise fitting the denominator also adds the sum of every other item's weight, so the correction is diluted by the other feedback. The proof shows that directional constraints "move further", but moving further is not the same as moving correctly; that has to be tested by experiment.

## 2. Method: four steps

The first step computes each feedback item's new direction. All vectors are L2-normalized and lie on the unit sphere. For a feedback vector $f_i$, compute its similarity to the query $s_i=q^\top f_i$, then remove the part parallel to the query to get $r_i=f_i-s_iq$. The direction $u_i$ of $r_i$ is where this feedback wants to rotate the query, and its length $\ell_i$ equals the sine of the angle between them, measuring how much the feedback brings that the original query lacks. The authors deliberately separate "how much is new" ($\ell_i$) from "how trustworthy" (decided by $s_i$), so that "very different from the query" is not mistaken for "informative and trustworthy".

The second step scores each feedback item's confidence. Confidence $\tau_i=g\cdot a_i$ has two levels. Item quality $a_i$: the $s_i$ of all feedback for the same query are standardized by their median and median absolute deviation, then passed through a sigmoid. Feedback closer to the query gets more weight, and the score does not depend on the absolute similarity scale of a given model. Set confidence $g$: compute the mean $\mu$ of all correction vectors, let $S=\lVert\mu\rVert^2$ be the strength of the mean direction and $V$ the average squared distance of each correction vector from $\mu$ (the spread); the geometric confidence is $g_{\text{geo}}=S/(S+V/K)$, with $K$ the number of feedback items, between 0 and 1. $g$ is high when the feedback agrees on a direction and low when it points every which way. It is finally multiplied by the set's average item quality, because a set of uniformly weak feedback can still agree with itself.

The third step solves for the correction jointly. The objective keeps only each feedback item's constraint along its own direction, plus a penalty on the size of the correction:

$$\delta^*=\arg\min_{\delta}\ \frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\delta\rVert^2+\frac12\sum_i\tau_i(u_i^\top\delta-\ell_i)^2$$

This has a closed-form solution requiring only a $K\times K$ linear system ($K$ is the number of feedback items, 5 in the main experiments), at a cost of $O(K^2D+K^3)$ where $D$ is the embedding dimension.

The fourth step maps the correction back to the sphere: the final rotation angle is the smaller of $\lVert\delta^*\rVert$ and "$g$ × the maximum allowed angle $\theta_{up}$", and $q'=\cos\phi\,q+\sin\phi\,\delta^*/\lVert\delta^*\rVert$. When the feedback set is untrustworthy, $g$ is small and the query barely moves.

## 3. Experiments

Setup: 14 BEIR subsets (including argument retrieval ArguAna, fact checking FEVER, multi-hop QA HotpotQA, MSMARCO, Google search questions NQ (Natural Questions), scientific claim verification SciFact, pandemic literature search TREC-COVID and others), and three retrievers: bge-base-en-v1.5, e5-base-v2 and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. There are two kinds of feedback: the top $K$ documents from first-pass retrieval (PRF), and three kinds of text generated by Qwen3.8-27B (HyDE hypothetical documents, Q2D query expansion, CoT reasoning). All methods share the same encoder, feedback and index; only the fusion method differs. Baselines include vector averaging (VPRF), concatenate-then-re-encode (Concat-P/L), OR-PRF which keeps only orthogonal components, DIME (per-dimension importance selection) and its refinement Eclipse, and AnchorQE, which needs extra retrieval to estimate weights.

### 3.1 Main results

The table gives average NDCG@10 over the 14 subsets; the original query's score without feedback is in parentheses:

| Retriever (original query) | Feedback | VPRF | OR-PRF | AnchorQE | DIFF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BGE (0.5492) | PRF | 0.5045 | 0.5392 | 0.5466 | **0.5522** |
| | HyDE | 0.5410 | 0.5606 | 0.5700 | **0.5717** |
| | Q2D | 0.5564 | 0.5632 | 0.5698 | **0.5723** |
| E5 (0.5231) | PRF | 0.4775 | 0.5103 | 0.5225 | **0.5252** |
| | HyDE | 0.5088 | 0.5189 | 0.5487 | **0.5489** |
| Qwen (0.5492) | PRF | 0.5066 | 0.5388 | 0.5459 | **0.5491** |
| | HyDE | 0.5607 | 0.5702 | 0.5720 | **0.5777** |

Two things stand out. First, with retrieved documents as feedback, plain averaging drags the score below the original query, from 0.5492 to 0.5045 on BGE; ==in this column DIFF merely avoids losing points==. The paper's own significance marks agree: on E5 and Qwen, DIFF's change relative to the original query is not significant, and only BGE's +0.003 is marked significant. Second, with LLM-generated feedback every method improves, and DIFF is very close to AnchorQE. On E5 + HyDE the gap is 0.0002 and with CoT feedback on BGE it is 0.0004, and the paper marks no significant difference in either cell. AnchorQE needs extra retrieval to estimate weights and DIFF does not; that is DIFF's practical advantage when the scores tie.

### 3.2 Per-query changes beneath the average

![Distribution of per-query NDCG@10 change under PRF feedback (paper appendix Figure 4a). The x-axis is the method's NDCG@10 minus the original query's. Blue VPRF has a large mass on the negative side; orange DIME and green DIFF both cluster at 0, DIFF most tightly.](figs/2610.29464/fig4a_delta_prf.png)

This figure explains why the PRF average barely moves. VPRF makes many queries clearly worse, with a batch losing 0.4 to 0.6. DIFF leaves the vast majority of queries essentially unchanged, with roughly as many getting better as worse. The reason is that retrieved documents point in scattered directions, so set confidence $g$ is low and step four squeezes the rotation angle to almost nothing. In other words, DIFF's behavior under noisy feedback is close to "don't move". That is robust, but it also means DIFF fails to pick out the useful few among the retrieved documents. The authors report that under HyDE feedback DIFF improves clearly more queries than it hurts, while still leaving many queries unchanged.

### 3.3 By subset: the gains concentrate in a few datasets

The appendix gives per-subset results on BGE. The table picks the subsets with the most visible changes:

| Subset | Original | DIFF (PRF) | DIFF (HyDE) | AnchorQE (HyDE) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NQ | 0.5411 | 0.5451 | 0.5962 | 0.5872 |
| TREC-COVID | 0.7802 | 0.8012 | 0.8480 | 0.8401 |
| DBPedia | 0.4078 | 0.4104 | 0.4429 | 0.4424 |
| FEVER | 0.8630 | 0.8541 | 0.8695 | 0.8723 |
| Touche2020 | 0.2571 | 0.2473 | 0.2646 | 0.2580 |
| Quora | 0.8874 | 0.8834 | 0.8832 | 0.8870 |
| ArguAna | 0.4534 | 0.4673 | 0.4550 | 0.4592 |

Under PRF, DIFF rises slightly on 10 subsets and drops slightly on 4. The largest gain is 0.021 on TREC-COVID and the largest drop 0.010 on Touche2020, so the average barely changes. Under HyDE the gains come mainly from QA and entity-retrieval tasks such as NQ, TREC-COVID and DBPedia, because the LLM's hypothetical answers resemble the target documents in style. Quora is duplicate-question retrieval, where a hypothetical answer does not match the target's genre, and DIFF ends up slightly below the original query. Subset by subset, under HyDE DIFF beats AnchorQE on 10 subsets and loses on 4.

### 3.4 Ablations

On BGE, one component is removed or replaced at a time:

| Variant | PRF NDCG@10 | HyDE NDCG@10 |
|---|---|---|
| Full DIFF | 0.5522 | 0.5717 |
| Back to pointwise fitting (weighted sum of corrections) | 0.5439 | 0.5646 |
| No confidence at all (τ=1) | 0.5454 | 0.5703 |
| No item quality (a=1) | 0.5462 | 0.5481 |
| Item quality without median normalization | 0.5487 | 0.5684 |
| No set confidence (g=1) | 0.5483 | 0.5565 |

Reverting to pointwise fitting is among the largest drops, which supports the paper's central claim. Under PRF, though, every variant in the table falls below the original query's 0.5492, and only full DIFF is above it, by 0.003. So the components mainly bring the loss down to zero rather than producing a gain. Under HyDE, removing item quality drops the score from 0.5717 to 0.5481, showing that generated hypothetical documents vary in quality and must be treated differently.

### 3.5 Hyperparameters and efficiency

DIFF has two hyperparameters: the pull back toward the original query $\lambda$ and the maximum rotation angle $\theta_{up}$, searched on a 3×3 grid. Under PRF the 9 results range from 0.5452 to 0.5522, only 5 of them above the original query. The best setting uses the small angle π/12, which again says the best strategy with retrieved feedback is to barely move. Under HyDE the 9 results range from 0.5631 to 0.5717, and only 2 beat AnchorQE's 0.5700. The paper does not say which data the grid search used. If settings were picked directly on the test set, DIFF's lead over AnchorQE lies within this range of variation.

On efficiency, timed on 10 queries, DIFF takes 0.258 seconds, on par with vector averaging at 0.247 seconds, while AnchorQE takes 3.67 times as long as DIFF because of its extra retrieval. But 10 queries is a tiny sample, good only for the order of magnitude.

## 4. Limitations

The main one is in the main table and the distribution plot: with first-pass retrieved documents as feedback, DIFF gains almost nothing over the original query; its value is "not being dragged down by noise". Next, the lead over AnchorQE with generated feedback is small and may depend on hyperparameter choice, and the paper reports no variance across runs. Also, experiments are only on BEIR, the largest retriever is 0.6B, and there is no validation on production-scale corpora or larger embedding models. Generated feedback also comes from a single LLM.

## 5. Practical implications

If your system already uses HyDE or query expansion and averages the encoded generated text with the original query, consider switching to DIFF. It relies only on the vectors, needs no training and no extra retrieval, and adds one 5×5 linear solve per query, matching AnchorQE without extra retrieval calls. Before rollout, evaluate separately by query type: for tasks like Quora's "find similar questions", a hypothetical answer is the wrong kind of text to begin with. If your feedback comes from first-pass retrieval results, this paper suggests the gain is limited. Treat DIFF as insurance against averaging dragging your metrics down, not as a source of improvement.

papers.title: Scan or Index? large Evidence Coverage, Answer Quality, and Cost in Long-Document RAG
papers.authors: Juan Terven, Diana-Margarita C\'ordova-Esparza, Julio-Alejandro Romero-Gonz\'alez, Edgar Chavez-Urbiola, Juan Irving Vasquez, Julian Andres Ramirez-Bautista, Silvia L. Chaparro-C\'ardenas, Gendry Alfonso-Francia
papers.summary: For long-document QA, should you build a vector index then retrieve, or let the model scan the full text segment by segment each time? The authors compare 11 setups on 396 QASPER paper questions and 80 questions from 8 full textbooks, fixing chunking, a top-5 segment budget, and the same answer model. On textbooks, hybrid retrieval plus Jev reranking reaches the highest evidence coverage (94.1%), Jev full-text scan 88.7%, and OpenAI vector retrieval 81.3%: even though full-text scan sees every segment, ==later filtering drops relevant segments==. ==Higher evidence coverage does not mean better answers==; the highest answer accuracy is hybrid retrieval plus OpenAI Decisions reranking (0.892). When queries are many, a reusable vector index costs the least.

papers.title: An Explicit Feedback Contract for Iterative ML-Agent Harnesses
papers.authors: Kehui Yao, Chuanbo Hu, Jiao Chen, Ramin Giahi, Reza Yousefi Maragheh, Lalitesh Morishetti, Ziwei Hong, Yiyun Su, Jianpeng Xu, Evren Korpeoglu, Kannan Achan
papers.summary: When an ML agent edits code, runs experiments, reads validation scores, and chooses the next step, it keeps changes that happen to look better on that validation set. Walmart defines a feedback rule for this loop: only tell the agent the validation score when the lift over the current best exceeds a noise threshold from paired standard error, and specify when to stop and when the test set may be touched. On a ==control task constructed so no real lift is possible==, an agent that sees exact scores reports a final lift of 0.0157, versus 0.0033 under the rule. On Criteo CTR and MSLR ranking, validation–test gaps shrink and test scores are slightly higher; with exact scores 2 of 3 tasks use all 30 submissions, while the rule stops at 4–12.

papers.title: How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage
papers.summary: This NVIDIA tutorial shows how to use KvikIO in Python to read files straight into GPU memory without a CPU bounce buffer (GPUDirect Storage). ==Each read takes two routing decisions==: KvikIO first chooses cuFile or its own POSIX-compatible path, and reads below a threshold (16 KiB in the tutorial) go POSIX; cuFile then chooses the nvidia-fs accelerated path or a CPU-mediated compatibility path. The two choices are controlled by KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE, KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD, and parallel-split settings in cufile.json. To confirm the accelerated path ran, set CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 and check whether gds_stats counts land in the nvfs or posix column.

papers.title: The science behind TorchNeuron, Amazon’s new PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium chips
papers.summary: TorchNeuron is Amazon's open-source PyTorch backend for running models on Trainium. Optional adaptive eager mode batches operators into small graphs that a background compiler compiles, caches, and queues, picking a split strategy by graph size so ==compilation overlaps with execution of already-compiled work== and approaches full-graph compile speed. Artifacts use memory and disk caches, and accelerators on one server share a compile service; on a large cross-accelerator model, time to the first training step falls by about one third. For testing, an AI agent picks 841 representative models by structural features from hundreds of thousands on Hugging Face for tuning and regression.

papers.title: Running Frontier-Class AI Models Across 8 NVIDIA DGX Spark Nodes
papers.summary: NVIDIA announces that DGX Spark officially supports an 8-node cluster, each with 128 GB unified memory (1 TB total), enough to run full GLM 5.3 locally (753B, ~470 GB in NVFP4): about 1,600 token/s single-concurrency prefill and 31 token/s decode. Under switch networking, the RoCEnante collective backend ==cuts all-reduce latency in tensor-parallel decode==, raising the 8-node decode speedup from 3.05× to 4.43×. Pretraining nanochat from scratch on 8 nodes speeds up 7.79× with 97.4% scaling efficiency.

papers.title: PACE: Periodic and Channel-Aligned Encoding of Four-Bit Recurrent States
papers.authors: Patrick Haller, Filipe Laitenberger, Alan Akbik
papers.summary: Linear-attention models keep a fixed-size recurrent state per decoding sequence; the cheaper the state, the more sequences one GPU can serve. Prior work quantizes the state every token and quality drops sharply at 4 bits. PACE quantizes every few tokens and buffers the in-between tokens; it also finds that ==large values in gated delta state cluster by column, so each column shares one quantization scale==; a few heads that accumulate error keep 8 bits. On four hybrid models from 4B to 35B, a 4/8-bit mix matches 8-bit DAMP on the three larger models at about two-thirds the memory; pure 4-bit beats Q-Mamba at equal memory.

papers.title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
papers.authors: Qiuyang Mang, Wenhao Chai, Runyuan He, Dongruixuan Li, Zihan Zheng
papers.summary: FrontierCS 2 tests whether AI agents can do computer-science research: take a paper and the authors' public code, remove the paper's core contribution, and require the agent to reimplement it in that repo and beat the removed original. Forty-eight tasks span 13 areas including ML systems, HPC, databases, security, and robotics; agents may submit patches anytime for a dev-set score and are judged on a held-out test set against the original. Among 12 agents, Claude Opus 5.5 is best with 58% of runs passing; 16 tasks see no passing run. ==Runs whose aggregate score beats the original still usually miss some metric or workload==.

papers.title: MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory
papers.summary: Memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to store before a question arrives; coding agents keep the raw dialogue and let the model search with tools. On one LoCoMo dialogue (419 turns, 152 questions) the authors run four memory methods (full context, BM25, Mem0, Zep) and three coding agents (Pi, Codex, Claude Code) with GPT-4o-mini, GPT-6 Luna, and Claude Opus 5.5, logging cost each time. Mem0 beats full context only under GPT-4o-mini, and ==building the memory alone costs more than one full-context QA==; with Claude Opus 5.5, Pi answers 99% correctly at under half the full-context cost. Each combo is run once; the authors note the study is small.
